title: Depala vas affair and dismissal as Minister of Defence (1994)
description: On the evening of 20 March 1994 members of the Defence Ministry, including its security service (VOMO) and the special brigade Moris, arrested Milan Smolnikar, described by 24ur as a covert police collaborator, at Depala vas. According to the later indictment of four ministry employees, rifle butts were used to smash the front windows of his car, injuring him, and he was handcuffed and held at the security service's premises before being taken to hospital. Prime Minister Janez Drnovšek dismissed Janša, defence minister since 1990, the same month, and his party then left the governing coalition; 24ur called the affair 'notorious and never properly explained'. In 1996 the head of the state prosecutors for special cases, Barbara Brezigar, dismissed the police's criminal complaints; after Smolnikar's lawyer obtained a judicial investigation, the four employees were indicted in January 2001. They said they had acted with the knowledge of their superiors and within their powers. Janša was not charged. In March 2003 he presented documents that he said proved the affair had been a prepared political action, including a February 1994 draft police plan to counter alleged Defence Ministry activities 'aimed at keeping Minister Janša in office contrary to the constitution and laws', which he called 'essentially a secret plan for civil war'.
key_facts: 20 March 1994: Milan Smolnikar arrested by Defence Ministry personnel
Janša dismissed as defence minister the same month; his party left the coalition
Complaints dismissed in 1996; four ministry employees indicted in January 2001 at Smolnikar's initiative
Janša was not charged; in 2003 he presented documents he said showed a political operation against him

title: Anti-corruption commission report on his assets and the fall of his second government (2013)
description: On 8 January 2013 the Commission for the Prevention of Corruption (KPK) published its report on the assets of the leaders of parliamentary parties, finding breaches of anti-corruption law by Prime Minister Janša and by Positive Slovenia leader Zoran Janković; for Janša it found that his assets had grown by at least €210,000 more than his known official income explained. The report triggered a government crisis and the break-up of his coalition, and on 27 February 2013 the National Assembly replaced him with Alenka Bratušek in a constructive vote of no confidence, 55 to 33. Janša challenged the report in court (see justice): in June 2014 the Supreme Court set aside the Administrative Court's dismissal of his lawsuit, which he called 'a big slap in the face for the KPK', adding that 'two governments fell because of it'; in February 2015 the Supreme Court annulled the report because it had not been sent to him for comment beforehand. The KPK repeated the review and in June 2015 again found an unexplained increase of €210,000, which it said had co-financed property purchases, an upmarket car and private travel; it also listed items he had not reported on time, such as a 2005 flat purchase, a €135,000 mortgage taken in 2009 and a guarantee for a loan to the SDS. Janša called the new draft unlawful and asked for the calculation behind the figure.
key_facts: 8 January 2013: KPK report finds an unexplained increase in assets of at least €210,000
27 February 2013: constructive no-confidence vote, 55–33; Alenka Bratušek elected
February 2015: Supreme Court annulled the report on procedural grounds
June 2015: repeated KPK review again found €210,000 unexplained; Janša disputed it

title: Suspension of public funding for the Slovenian Press Agency (STA) and media-freedom concerns (2020–2021)
description: In October 2020 Janša called the national news agency STA a 'national disgrace' on Twitter, after it gave more space to an interview with a musician critical of the government than to his meeting with Viktor Orbán (Euronews). In December 2020 the head of the Government Communication Office, Uroš Urbanija, said the government could not finance the STA or sign a new public-service contract for 2021 because its management had not provided the company's accounts; the government said no formal decision to suspend funding had been taken, and the STA's chief supervisor rejected the claim that the agency had concealed information. The annual payment of about €2 million was suspended; under pressure from the EU, the government said in January 2021 that it had resumed payments. On 30 September 2021, during Slovenia's EU Council presidency, STA director Bojan Veselinović resigned, saying the agency had 'been working for free for 273 days' and that the government sought to 'subordinate' it; Janša had been calling for his resignation. The European Commission urged the government 'to take decisive action to stop and reverse the current trend'. Euronews reported that Janša had been accused of attacking journalists on Twitter and undermining press freedom since returning to power in 2020; the government presented the dispute as a legal and contractual one.
key_facts: October 2020: Janša called the STA a 'national disgrace'
December 2020: government communication office said it could not finance the STA for 2021
30 September 2021: STA director resigned, citing 273 days without payment
European Commission urged Slovenia to 'stop and reverse the current trend'

title: Delay in nominating Slovenia's European delegated prosecutors (2021)
description: The selection of Slovenia's two European delegated prosecutors for the new European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) was completed in December 2020, but the Janša government annulled the procedure in May 2021, so Slovenia had none when the EPPO started work on 1 June 2021. European Chief Prosecutor Laura Kövesi described Slovenia's approach as lacking 'sincere cooperation'. When Slovenia's EU Council presidency was presented in the European Parliament on 6 July 2021, several MEPs urged Janša to make the appointments; he said he would do so by the autumn, blamed procedural delays and pointed to member states that had not joined the EPPO at all. On 20 July 2021 Justice Commissioner Didier Reynders said the Commission would 'think about a possible procedure before the court'. On 24 November 2021 the EPPO College appointed two European delegated prosecutors from Slovenia for five-year terms.
key_facts: Selection completed in December 2020; procedure annulled by the government in May 2021
EPPO began work on 1 June 2021 without Slovenian delegated prosecutors
July 2021: Commissioner Reynders raised possible court action
24 November 2021: EPPO College appointed two Slovenian delegated prosecutors

title: Western Balkans 'non-paper' on redrawing borders attributed to him (2021)
description: In April 2021 the Slovenian portal Necenzurirano.si published a 'non-paper' proposing the dissolution of Bosnia and Herzegovina along ethnic lines, the joining of Serb- and Croat-majority territories to Serbia and Croatia and the unification of Kosovo and Albania. Media in the region attributed the document to Janša, who denied it; according to European Western Balkans, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said he had seen the document, while Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić denied seeing it. The EU delegation in Sarajevo restated its commitment to Bosnia and Herzegovina's territorial integrity, the European Commission and Council said they had received no such proposal, and Slovenian President Borut Pahor's office said he regularly warns against redrawing borders in the Western Balkans. The document's authenticity and origin were never established.
key_facts: Document published by Necenzurirano.si in April 2021
Attributed by regional media to Janša, who denied authorship
EU institutions said they had received no such proposal; authenticity never established

title: Black Cube affair: secret recordings before the 2026 election
description: In the weeks before the parliamentary election of 22 March 2026, secretly recorded conversations with several Slovenian political and business figures, suggesting corrupt practices and influence on decision-makers, were published on anonymous online channels. On 16 March the weekly Mladina reported that representatives of the Israeli private intelligence firm Black Cube had been in Slovenia. On 18 March, after the secretariat of the National Security Council discussed a report by the intelligence agency SOVA, state secretary Vojko Volk said the facts pointed to direct foreign interference in the election, 'most likely commissioned from Slovenia', that Black Cube representatives had been in Slovenia four times in six months, and that on 11 December 2025 three of them, Giora Eiland, Liron Tzur and Dan Zorella, had made a long stop on Trstenjakova street in Ljubljana, where the SDS has its headquarters. Janša confirmed meeting Giora Eiland, whom RTV SLO describes as one of Black Cube's leading representatives, 'at our place' but said he did not remember the date; he said SOVA kept a covert flat opposite the party headquarters, which SOVA denied, and he denies any unlawful cooperation with Black Cube. Mladina journalist Borut Mekina said in April that, as far as he knew, police had at least one source who had seen a meeting between Janša and Black Cube founder Dan Zorella; RTV SLO noted that, as far as was known, neither the SDS nor Janša was a party to any proceedings in the case. In June 2026 SDS MP Žan Mahnič said there was no evidence that Black Cube had made the recordings, and the chair of the parliamentary intelligence oversight committee announced an inspection of the police over the data passed to prosecutors. The opposition has repeatedly sought an extraordinary session to order parliamentary inquiries into the affair and into alleged indirect party financing; in October 2026 it withdrew one such request, saying the coalition and Resni.ca were blocking the inquiries and announcing a constitutional challenge to the Assembly's rules of procedure, while SDS deputy Zvonko Černač called the withdrawal 'a smart and reasonable decision' (N1).
key_facts: Recordings published anonymously before the 22 March 2026 election
18 March 2026: SOVA report to the National Security Council secretariat points to foreign interference
Janša confirmed meeting Giora Eiland and denies unlawful cooperation with Black Cube
No proceedings against Janša or the SDS reported in the sources reviewed
Opposition requests for a parliamentary inquiry not acted on as of October 2026

title: Reversal of Slovenia's policy towards Israel and Palestine, and the constitutional-indictment motion (2026)
description: Less than an hour after his election on 22 May 2026, Janša had the Palestinian flag lowered from a government building. His government then revoked the measures taken against Israel by the Golob government, which had recognised a Palestinian state in 2024, called Israel's war in Gaza a 'genocide' and imposed travel bans on Benjamin Netanyahu and two of his ministers; at the end of August 2026 Slovenia prevented the adoption of an EU joint statement condemning the conduct of Israeli settlers in the West Bank, and Israel opened a resident embassy in Ljubljana. Janša wrote that the 'politically and economically harmful period of government support for activist anti-Semitism' had ended. On 9 September 2026 the Freedom Movement and the Left filed a motion for a constitutional indictment, asking the Constitutional Court to remove him from office; Robert Golob said the government pursued a foreign policy 'exclusively in Israel's interest', and the motion alleges breaches of the Constitution, the Foreign Affairs Act and international law. Passing it requires 46 votes. The Social Democrats declined to co-sign and announced an interpellation of Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer instead; Kajzer has said Slovenia would pursue a pragmatic foreign policy following its own interests. In October 2026 the motion was not placed on the National Assembly's agenda after its legislative service found its content inadequate, and the Freedom Movement agreed it would be revised (N1).
key_facts: 22 May 2026: Palestinian flag removed from a government building
Golob government's measures against Israel revoked; EU statement on West Bank settlers blocked in August 2026
9 September 2026: Freedom Movement and the Left filed a constitutional-indictment motion (46 votes needed)
October 2026: motion not scheduled after the legislative service's opinion

title: Draft media and RTV Slovenija laws and halted media-support calls (2026)
description: On 26 August 2026 the Ministry of Culture published draft amendments to the RTV Slovenija Act and the Media Act. The RTV draft would turn the broadcaster's council back into a programme council and its finance committee into a seven-member supervisory board, six of whose members would be appointed by the government and which would appoint a single director-general in place of the current four-member management; the mandates of the existing bodies would end when the law took effect. The ministry says the draft 'continues the depoliticisation' of RTV's governance, as the programme council's members would be appointed by civil-society organisations without state bodies. The media draft would overhaul state support for media, abolish some forms of aid and delete provisions on influencers and misdemeanour sanctions for incitement to violence or hatred in the media; the ministry also stopped calls for media support already published under the existing law. According to 24ur, the drafts drew warnings of financial uncertainty and of the political subordination of the media, particularly the public broadcaster. Janša has said RTV Slovenija is governed and funded inefficiently and accused it of taking part in the referendum campaign without registering.
key_facts: 26 August 2026: draft RTV Slovenija Act and Media Act amendments published
Proposed RTV supervisory board with six of seven members appointed by the government
Existing media-support calls halted by the Ministry of Culture
Critics warned of political subordination of the public broadcaster; the ministry speaks of depoliticisation

title: Amendment to the Parliamentary Inquiries Act rejected in a referendum (2026)
description: In mid-May 2026, before Janša was elected Prime Minister, SDS and NSi–SLS–Fokus deputies tabled an amendment to the Parliamentary Inquiries Act (ZPPre-B), which the National Assembly adopted on 26 May 2026. Among other things it limits the possibility of challenging an act ordering a parliamentary inquiry before the Constitutional Court; its sponsors called the existing rules ineffective, and the government said the safeguards for those investigated introduced by the previous government 'cause serious delays in setting up an inquiry committee' (RTV SLO). The referendum's initiators argued that it removed basic safeguards of the rule of law and opened the way to political abuse, and they collected 44,619 voters' signatures in less than a month. On 11 October 2026 voters rejected the law, with 51.26% against and 48.74% for.
key_facts: Law adopted on 26 May 2026; referendum called on 23 July 2026 after 44,619 signatures
Critics argued it removed safeguards for people under parliamentary investigation
11 October 2026: rejected, 51.26% against
